quantity: Joint moments of ζ and its derivatives: ∫_T^{2T}|ζ|^{2k−2h}|ζ′|^{2h} ≍ T(log T)^{k^2+2h}
statement: Curran–Heycock, Theorem 1.1: for n ∈ Z_{>0}, 0 ≤ k ≤ 2, h_j ≥ 0 and h = Σh_j ≤ k, ∫_T^{2T} |ζ(1/2+it)|^{2k−2h} ∏_j |ζ^{(j)}(1/2+it)|^{2h_j} dt ≪ T(log T)^{k^2+2Σ j h_j}. This is unconditional for k ≤ 2 and assumes RH for k > 2. Theorem 1.2 (unconditional): for k ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ h < k+1/2, ∫_T^{2T} |ζ|^{2k−2h}|ζ′|^{2h} ≫ T(log T)^{k^2+2h}. The asymptotic is known only for integers 0 ≤ h ≤ k ≤ 2 (Ingham; Conrey 1988).
value: Sharp order unconditionally for 0 ≤ h ≤ k ≤ 2. Lower bound for all k ≥ 0, 0 ≤ h < k+1/2. Upper bound for all 0 ≤ h ≤ k on RH.
conditional_on: Upper bound for k > 2 assumes RH. The ranges stated as unconditional need no hypothesis.
location: Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, p.2. History on p.1.

history.value: fourth moment of derivatives (asymptotics, integer h ≤ k = 2); explicit ∫|ζ|^3|ζ′| ≥ (1+o(1))(173/(672π^2))T(log T)^5
sharp lower bounds for ∫|ζ′|^{2k}, all real k ≥ 0

caveats: The RMT constants C(k,h) involve Painlevé III/V transcendents. Explicit lower constants for integer joint moments are in Durkan–Page 2026 (MOM-10). Recent RMT conjectures for complex and mixed derivative moments at zeros (Hughes–Pearce-Crump, arXiv 2509.07788 and 2509.07792) are conjectural.

source.title: Sharp bounds for joint moments of the Riemann zeta function

quantity: Shifted moments M_{α,β}(T) = ∫_T^{2T} ∏_k |ζ(1/2+i(t+α_k))|^{2β_k} dt
statement: Curran, Theorem 1.1: assume RH. If β_k ≥ 0 and |α_k| ≤ T/2, then M_{α,β}(T) ≪_β T(log T)^{β_1^2+...+β_m^2} ∏_{j<k} |ζ(1 + i(α_j−α_k) + 1/log T)|^{2β_jβ_k}. Curran (arXiv 2405.08725, RH) proves the matching lower bound. Unconditionally (as summarized on p.1): β = (1/2,1/2) is handled by Atkinson's formula and Bettin (shifts up to T^{2−ε}); β = (1,1) by Motohashi and Kovaleva (shifts up to T^{3/2−ε}); and for β = (β,β), Curran proved sharp upper bounds for β ≤ 1 and lower bounds for all β, with shifts up to T^{1/2−ε}.
value: sharp order on RH for all β, |α| ≤ T/2. Unconditional sharp upper bounds only for total weight in the HRS range.
location: Theorem 1.1, p.2. Unconditional history on pp.1–2.

history.value: lower bounds for integer β; upper bounds on RH up to (log T)^ε
general α, β on RH (upper and lower)

caveats: Conditional on RH. Shifted-moment bounds are the key input in Ng–Shen–Wong's conditional eighth moment (MOM-13). Analogues for Dedekind zeta functions under GRH (Durkan–Karak–Mahatab, arXiv 2606.27516) and for products of GL(1)/GL(2) L-functions (Hagen, arXiv 2609.11619) concern other L-functions, not classical ζ.

source.title: Correlations of the Riemann zeta function

quantity: Largest height H to which RH for zeta is verified by a rigorous (interval/ball-arithmetic) refereed computation
statement: Unconditional, rigorous computation. Every nontrivial zero beta+i*gamma of zeta(s) with 0<gamma<=3,000,175,332,800 has beta=1/2. Equivalently, the lowest 12,363,153,437,138 nontrivial zeros lie on Re s=1/2. Method: Platt's windowed Booker/FFT evaluation of the completed zeta function on the half-line, reimplemented in Arb ball arithmetic in place of MPFI. On-line zeros are counted from sign changes. Completeness comes from Turing's method in Trudgian's 2011 and 2016 versions. No zero was isolated beyond detecting its sign change. About 7.5 million core hours on 3.6 GHz Xeons; sampling about 25 points per zero.
location: Theorem 1, p.2 of arXiv v1; computational details in Section 2, pp.2-3; Corollary 2 (Lambda<=0.2) in Section 3.4, p.5

history.authors: van de Lune, te Riele, Winter
history.note: refereed, classical floating-point error analysis (see VERIF-06)
first interval-arithmetic verification at this scale (VERIF-02)
about 98x Platt 2017 and about 5500x the 1986 height; 22% above Gourdon's unrefereed H

caveats: (1) Theorem 1 asserts beta=1/2 only. It does not state that the zeros are simple; rigorous simplicity is stated only up to 3.06e10 (VERIF-02). (2) The zbMATH review (Zbl 1482.11111) notes that no permanent link to the code is given. (3) I found no independent rigorous replication as of 2026-11-17. The authors say it independently confirms the non-rigorous results of Gourdon, Wedeniwski and Franke et al. (4) Rigor is relative to correct implementation, hardware and compiler. No certificate exists that is cheaper to check than the computation itself (Gourdon 2004, Section 1.1). (5) Searches (arXiv API, zbMATH, web) found no larger rigorous H published 2021-2026. This is a search result, not proof that none exists. (6) Applications: Corollary 2 gives Lambda<=0.2 using Polymath15 Table 1 (needs H>2.51e12). Johnston (arXiv 2109.02249) derives explicit prime-counting bounds from this H.

source.title: The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3*10^12

quantity: Rigorously isolated zeros of zeta to high precision (and certified simplicity)
statement: Every nontrivial zero rho with |Im rho|<=3.0610046e10 is simple and has Re rho=1/2. The 103,800,788,359 zeros with 0<Im s<30,610,046,000 were isolated to absolute precision +-2^-102 using about 6e12 high-precision evaluations (MPFI, 300-bit working precision) of a windowed Booker/Odlyzko-Schoenhage-type FFT algorithm. Completeness comes from Turing's method with Trudgian's Theorem 2.2. The ordinates (1.3 TB) are distributed through the LMFDB.
location: Theorem 5.1 and the paragraph before it, Section 5 (p.~10 of the Bristol author-accepted manuscript); error bounds in Appendix A
caveats: Read from the Bristol author-accepted manuscript (research-information.bris.ac.uk), not the AMS version of record. Tao (arXiv 1201.6656, proof of Theorem 1.5) cites this H as 3.06e10 and deliberately uses the more conservative T0=3.29e9, which he describes as checked by four independent computations. This is the only rigorous dataset of individually located zeros at this scale. Platt-Trudgian 2021 did not store or refine zeros.

source.title: Isolating some non-trivial zeros of zeta

quantity: Gourdon's floating-point verification of the first 10^13 zeros (unrefereed)
statement: Unrefereed preprint, not interval arithmetic. Using an optimized Odlyzko-Schoenhage algorithm in hardware floating point with explicit error bounds (Turing's method with the bound int S <= 2.30+0.128 log(t2/2pi)), the first 10^13 nontrivial zeros were found to lie on the critical line; Platt-Trudgian and Tao give H about 2.44e12. The run took the equivalent of 525 days of a 2.4 GHz Pentium 4 in 2003, averaged 1.193 evaluations of Z per zero, and was checked by sampling Riemann-Siegel values against Odlyzko-Schoenhage output and by a full rerun with different parameters. The same paper reports 2 billion zeros at each height 10^n for 13<=n<=24, including from the 10^24-th zero.
location: Section 3 (pp.19-25), Section 3.3.1 'Computation information' p.22; history table p.2; Section 4 p.25

history.value: 250e9 zeros per Gourdon's table (heights disputed, see VERIF-04)

caveats: (1) Never published in a refereed journal. Platt-Trudgian 2021 (p.2) say it is 'not clear how the computations were set up to avoid problematic accumulation of rounding and truncation errors', citing concerns by Tao and Helfgott. Superseded rigorously by VERIF-01. (2) Gourdon himself notes that verification costs as much as the computation and that such results are hard to regard as 'proved' in the strong sense (Section 1.1). (3) The Gram-block and Rosser statistics in the same paper are described there as 'not completely rigorous', because Gram points with undecidable sign were perturbed. (4) The paper's Turing bound 2.30+0.128 log(t/2pi) equals about 2.065+0.128 log t, consistent with Turing's triple (2.07, 0.128) as cited by Trudgian 2011.

source.title: The 10^13 first zeros of the Riemann Zeta function, and zeros computation at very large height

quantity: ZetaGrid (Wedeniwski) and Franke et al. claimed verification heights: disputed or unclear
statement: Distributed computation (ZetaGrid, 2001-2005) using plain Riemann-Siegel; unrefereed. Platt-Trudgian document inconsistent claims. Slides of 20 May 2003 claim 200 billion zeros (H=5.72e10). The end of the same slides claims 385 billion (H=1.07e11). Slides of 12 Nov 2003 claim 561 billion (H=1.53e11). A Wikipedia link gives 900 billion (the frequently quoted H=2.41e11). Franke, Kleinjung, Buethe and Jost (Math. Comp. 86 (2017)) claim H=10^11 with few computational details.
value: claimed H between 5.72e10 and 2.41e11 (inconsistent sources); Franke et al. H=1e11
location: footnote 1, pp.1-2, and p.2 paragraph on Franke et al. [9]
caveats: I did not access Wedeniwski's original slides; this entry depends on Platt-Trudgian's footnote and Tao's remark. All these claims fall below the rigorous H of VERIF-01, so the dispute is now only historical. Gourdon (p.3) notes that ZetaGrid's classical method 'is more likely to control potential numerical errors'.

source.authors: D. Platt, T. Trudgian (documenting S. Wedeniwski's ZetaGrid slides)
source.title: The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3*10^12 (footnote 1)

quantity: Brent 1979 verification (H(75,000,001)) and the early verification ladder
statement: Brent (1979): zeta(s) has exactly 75,000,000 zeros with 0<t<32,585,736.4; all are simple and on sigma=1/2, so H(75,000,001) holds. The method is Lehmer-style Riemann-Siegel evaluation with Gram blocks, Rosser's rule and Turing's theorem. Brent's introduction lists earlier results: Gram H(10), Backlund H(79), Hutchinson H(138) and Titchmarsh-Comrie H(1,041) by hand; then Lehmer H(25,000) on a digital computer, Meller H(35,337), Lehman H(250,000), and Rosser-Yohe-Schoenfeld H(3,500,000). Table 3 lists all 15 exceptions to Rosser's rule up to Gram block B_75,000,000, the first at n=13,999,525.

quantity: Complexity exponent for evaluating zeta(1/2+it) to +-t^{-lambda}
statement: Unconditional theorem (algorithmic). For any fixed lambda, zeta(1/2+it) can be computed to within +-t^{-lambda} using at most A1 (log t)^kappa1 t^{4/13} operations on numbers of at most A2 (log t)^2 bits. This requires a one-time precomputation of at most A3 (log t)^kappa2 t^{4/13} operations and at most A4 (log t)^kappa3 t^{4/13} bits of storage. With little storage, the exponent is 1/3 (Hiary, quadratic exponential sums). Amortized: Hiary's elementary method evaluates zeta at any floor(T^{1/4}) points of [T, T+T^{1/4}] in average time T^{1/4+o(1)} per point. Odlyzko-Schoenhage (1988) computes about T^{1/2} values in time T^{1/2+eps}, so verification to height H costs about H^{1+o(1)}.

No published 2011-2026 improvement of 4/13 was found. A faster single-point algorithm does not reduce the cost of full verification, which is dominated by the about H log H zeros.

quantity: Theorems on Gram's law, the Weak Gram law and Rosser's rule (infinitely often / positive proportion)
statement: Unconditional theorems. For sufficiently large T, a positive proportion of the Gram intervals (g_n, g_{n+1}] in [T,2T] contain no zero of zeta(1/2+it). Hence Gram's law (exactly one zero per Gram interval) and the Weak Gram law (at least one zero) both fail for a positive proportion of intervals. A positive proportion of Gram intervals in [T,2T] contain at least one zero, so the Weak Gram law succeeds a positive proportion of the time. Earlier: Titchmarsh proved that Gram's law fails infinitely often and that the Weak Gram law holds infinitely often; Lehman (1970) first showed that Rosser's rule fails infinitely often.

quantity: Guth–Maynard large-values estimate for Dirichlet polynomials
statement: Hypotheses: |b_n| ≤ 1 (an ℓ∞ bound), (t_r)_{r≤R} 1-separated in [0,T], and |Σ_{n=N}^{2N} b_n n^{it_r}| ≥ V for every r. Conclusion: R ≤ T^{o(1)}(N^2V^{−2} + N^{18/5}V^{−4} + T N^{12/5}V^{−4}). This beats the classical MVT + Montgomery–Halász–Huxley bound R ≤ T^{o(1)}(N^2V^{−2} + T·min(NV^{−2}, N^4V^{−6})) exactly when N^{7/10+ε} < V < N^{8/10−ε} and N ≤ T^{5/6−ε}. In the key case N = T^{4/5}, V = N^{3/4} it gives R ≤ T^{13/25+o(1)} instead of T^{3/5}. The core result is Proposition 3.1: |W| ≤ T N^{(12−20σ)/5+o(1)} for W in an interval of length T = N^{6/5}. Larger T are reached by Huxley subdivision. Proposition 12.1 refines the bound for N ≥ T^{5/6}: R ⪅ N^{2−2σ} + T^{1/2}N^{3−4σ} + T^{(30σ−21)/5}N^{(46−60σ)/5}.
value: R ⪅ N^2V^{−2} + N^{18/5}V^{−4} + T N^{12/5}V^{−4}. At σ = 3/4, T = N^{6/5}: |W| ⪅ N^{0.6}, against N^{0.7} from the MVT and N^{0.5} conjectured (Montgomery).

quantity: Negative results and barriers for the large-values route to zero density
statement: (i) A(1/2) = 2 by Riemann–von Mangoldt (TTY eq. (27)), so the DH exponent 2 is optimal at σ = 1/2. (ii) LV(σ,τ) ≥ min(2−2σ, τ) (TTY Lemma 29; GM footnote 1 constructs |W| ≫ N^{2−2σ}), so Montgomery's large-values conjecture is sharp. (iii) Bourgain's counterexample to Montgomery's original ℓ2-normalised conjecture (GM p. 4; Guth §3.4). (iv) Bourgain: Montgomery's ℓq large-values conjecture implies the 'Bourgain–Kakeya' conjecture for fat arithmetic progressions, which implies the Kakeya conjecture in every dimension (Guth survey §9, p. 39). Guth notes that assuming Bourgain–Kakeya as a black box currently gives no LV improvement. (v) Partial converse (Matomäki–Teräväinen 2024; TTY Lemma 40): zero-density bounds imply ζ-large-value bounds, so better A(σ) cannot bypass LV_ζ. (vi) Computational barrier: for planted large-value problems, low-degree tests cannot beat the operator-norm bound in a parameter range (Mao–Wein, per Guth §8). There is no meaningful numerical evidence for the LV conjectures even at N = 200 (Guth §4).
value: Floors: A(1/2) = 2 and LV ≥ min(2−2σ, τ); DH via the ℓq LV conjecture is at least as hard as Kakeya in all dimensions
location: Guth §3.4–3.5 (pp. ~10–12), §4 (p. ~13), §9 (pp. 37–40, Conjecture 9.3 and Bourgain's implication on p. 39). TTY Lemma 29 (p. 16) and Lemma 40 (p. 25).

statement: Theorem 1.1 (OpenAI, 5 Oct 2026): every finite-order Hecke L-function over K = Q(sqrt(-3)) has no zeros in Re s > 11/12. Hence every Dirichlet L-function, including zeta(s), has no zeros for Re s > 11/12. The proof reduces to Proposition 3.1. Let A_u(D) = sum over n coprime to S of mu(n) nu(n) chi_n(u) W(N(n)/D), with sextic residue symbols chi_n(u) = (u/n)_6. For 0 < theta <= 1/10, Proposition 3.1 claims sum_{0<N(u)<=D^{1+theta}} |A_u(D)|^2 << D^{2+theta+eps}. Taking the rows u = p^6 with N(p) about Y = H^{1/6} gives |A_1(D)|^2 << D^{11/6+5theta/6+eps} + D^{5/3-theta/3}, so A_1(D) << D^{11/12+eps}. A Mellin argument then excludes zeros. Corollary 1.2: sup_{q<=x} |pi(x;q,a) - li(x)/phi(q)| << x^{11/12} log x, with an absolute, effective constant.

quantity: Negative result: optimality of the classical region (and of any wider contour) under Beurling hypotheses
statement: Diamond-Montgomery-Vorhauer (Math. Ann. 334, 2006) construct Beurling generalized prime systems whose integers satisfy N(x) = Ax + O(x^theta) with theta >= 1/2, yet whose zeta functions have zeros on a de la Vallee Poussin contour. Hence the classical region cannot be improved using only the Euler product plus integer-count regularity. Broucke (2025, Theorem 1.6) generalizes this. Let f be eventually C^1, decreasing and strictly convex, with 1/u = o(f(u)), and either regularly varying of index -alpha (0 < alpha <= 1) or slowly varying with (1.10). Then there is a Beurling system with N_P(x) = Ax + O_eps(x^{1/2+eps}) whose zeta has infinitely many zeros on sigma = 1 - f(log|t|) and none to the right. It also has a matching Omega_plus-minus PNT error term. Broucke-Revesz (arXiv:2611.03356) further show zeros near the 1-line must occur in clusters.

quantity: Negative/limit results for the trigonometric-polynomial and smoothing (zero-detector) method of the classical constant
statement: Landau's V = lim_n inf_{f in P_n} (f(0) - a0)/(sqrt(a1) - sqrt(a0))^2 controls the classical constant in the Landau/Stechkin method: R0 = V/2 + eps (Landau), R0 = (V/2)(1 - 1/sqrt5) + eps (Stechkin). Mossinghoff-Trudgian Theorem 2: 34.468305 < V < 34.4889920009. The lower bound is due to Arestov-Kondrat'ev 1990, so these methods cannot go below about 9.5. Smoothing (Heath-Brown 1992; Kadiri 2005) circumvents this barrier. BTY 2026 measure the efficiency c of the zero-detector weight: c = 1 for Heath-Brown's, 1.78 for Kadiri's, 1.98 for their discrete approximation, and c = 2 for the hypothetical optimal weight h(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-(2 sigma - 1)u}). They call their weight 'within one percent of the hypothetical limit of the method'.
value: 34.468305 < V < 34.4889920009; BTY efficiency 1.98 of a hypothetical maximum 2
location: MT 2015: eqs. (1.1)-(1.3), Theorem 2, p.3. BTY: Section 2, p.6, discussion after eq. (20).

history.value: optimal Landau polynomials of degrees 7 and 8 (numerical)

caveats: The 'efficiency' limit in BTY is a heuristic within their framework, not a theorem that R cannot go below a given value. Leong-Mossinghoff (arXiv:2404.05928) show 3 + 4cos + cos2 is optimal for Titchmarsh's lower bound of |zeta(sigma+it)| with sigma > 1, a related but distinct extremal problem.

quantity: Equivalence-type link between the zero-free region and the PNT error term (why the region matters)
statement: Pintz (1980): a zero-free region of VK type with constant c gives pi(x) - li(x) << x exp(-d (log x)^{3/5} (log log x)^{-1/5}), with d = (5^6/(2^2 3^4 c^2))^{1/5}, and conversely the error term determines the region. MTY: c = 48.1588 gives d >= 0.2123. Bellotti (arXiv:2508.02041) shows N(sigma,T) is bounded by an absolute constant near the left edge of the VK region. It then claims the optimal form psi(x) - x << x exp(-omega(x)) with omega(x) = min_t {nu(t) log x + log t}, i.e. epsilon = 0 in the Pintz-Johnston formulation.
value: d >= 0.2123 (with c = 48.1588); slightly larger with Bellotti's 48.0718
location: MTY Section 2, p.4. Bellotti 2508.02041 (abstract only).
